CHI 2027
Papers Review Process

31 August 2026chi2027.acm.org · Pittsburgh, PA

Good evening everyone. Tonight we're walking through how reviewing will work for CHI 2027 in Pittsburgh, and it changes quite a lot.

Everything in this deck comes from the official CHI 2027 site and the chairs' blog posts from May through August; I'll flag where numbers are official versus working targets. We'll walk the whole pipeline start to finish, then open it up for discussion. If you're planning a September 10 submission, this affects you directly.

Follow SwissCHI: LinkedIn · swisschi.acm.org · mailing list
Author: Prof April Wang | ETH Zurich | Adapted from the CHI 2027 official website and blog posts
Background

Why is the review process changing?

Some context on why CHI is doing this. [Left chart: four decades of submission counts: flat for 20 years, then a hockey stick.] CHI 2026 received 6,730 complete submissions, up 34% in a single year, 66% over two. Reviewing that took more than 24,000 reviews.

[Right chart: naive linear vs. exponential extrapolation with 95% prediction intervals; reality is probably somewhere between 8,500 and 26,000 by 2030. Either way, the old model doesn't survive it.]

The chairs' framing: full peer review is a scarce community resource. The old model sent about 86% of everything to full review, and that simply doesn't scale.

One thing worth stressing: they explicitly state there is no target acceptance rate and no cap on accepted papers. Screening is about where review effort goes, not about hitting a quota.

  • “… full peer review is a scarce community resource. Sending every submission to three external reviewers and an AC, including papers with no viable path to acceptance, creates an unsustainable burden on reviewers …”
  • “CHI 2027 is not aiming for a predetermined acceptance rate. It is also not aiming for a predetermined number of accepted papers.”
Source: “How the CHI 2027 Papers Review Process Will Work” (Aug 17)
Background

What is this information session about?

Before we dive in: what this session is, and what it isn't. First, the disclaimer: SwissCHI is an independent community organization. We are not representing the CHI 2027 organizing committee, and nothing tonight is an official interpretation.

Two caveats. The process is still evolving; some details have already changed between announcements: the August 29 post reversed part of the August 17 description (the announced AI-assisted ADR rubric will not actually be used). The process at a glance

Press → to walk the process step by step · click a stage region to jump to its slides · M brings you back anytime

Here's the whole process; I'll build it up step by step. [Keep pressing → as you talk; each press reveals the next stage.]

You submit September 10: the paper plus review slots and descriptors; more on both in a minute. An automated completeness check runs first and you get a window to fix issues. Then two gates with humans in charge: the classic desk reject for rule violations, and the new ADR (Assisted Desk Reject), a scholarly screen. Notifications for both land around October 25.

Papers that pass get full peer review (three external reviews plus an AC meta-review), released with first decisions on November 5. Three possible outcomes; revisions are due December 3. Minor revisions are checked by the AC alone; major ones go back to the reviewers. Final accept-or-reject on December 17.

All the key dates live on this map: submission Sep 10, screening notifications around Oct 25, reviews and first decisions Nov 5, revisions Dec 3, final decisions Dec 17. Plan backwards from Sep 10; review slots, ORCIDs, and descriptors are part of the submission, not an afterthought.

Stage 1 · Submission · Sep 10, 2026 (AoE)

Submitting a paper means sharing responsibility for review

The biggest cultural change: submitting now carries a formal reviewing obligation. Four slots per paper, each one a named, qualified author committing to one full review. The slots can be split across authors, and one person can take all four, as in the examples on the right; with one carve-out for AC-qualified coauthors that we'll see on the next slide.

Two things people will trip over. First, slots are locked at submission; you cannot transfer them later. Second, a teammate doing an extra review does not cover a review the named author missed.

There are exemptions: a team with no qualified reviewer declares that at submission, and parental leave or medical emergencies count; ordinary workload does not. And the other direction is fair too: if CHI never sends you enough review invitations, the affected slots count as fulfilled, no penalty. But if fulfillable slots go unfulfilled, the associated submission can be desk-rejected.

  • Each submission declares four review-responsibility slots Each slot is assigned to a qualified author of the paper, who commits to completing one CHI full-paper review.
  • The four slots can be distributed across eligible authors One author may take multiple slots; only authors of the submitted paper can be named. Subject to an additional requirement for AC-qualified coauthors → next slide.
  • Declared slots are non-transferable after submission The author named for a slot is responsible for completing that review; another co-author cannot complete an extra review to make up for a missed one.
  • Exemptions exist e.g., no qualified author on the team, parental leave, or medical emergency; ordinary workload is not an exemption.
  • No assignment, no penalty If CHI does not provide enough review invitations, the affected slots are treated as fulfilled.

Failure to fulfill the applicable review-responsibility requirements can lead to desk rejection of the associated submission(s).

One author covers all four
AAAAA reviews 4 papers
Four authors, one each
ABCD1 review each
Slots can be split across authors
AABB2 + 2
Source: “Submitting a CHI 2027 paper means sharing responsibility for peer review” (Aug 24)
Stage 1 · Submission · Sep 10, 2026 (AoE)

Who can take the review-responsibility slots?

Who can actually take these slots? The minimum bar: at least one full publication at CHI or a specialised SIGCHI conference, plus prior mentoring or training in review writing, with exceptions for relevant methodological or domain expertise or experience at another leading HCI venue.

And then: there is one additional detail that is easy to miss, because it appears later in the FAQ. If a paper has an AC-qualified coauthor, the Aug 24 FAQ says that author must take at least one slot; a reviewer-qualified student can take the other three, but the four slots cannot all go to the student. That's the example on the right: two valid splits, one invalid.

Important nuance: AC-qualified is about qualifications, not job titles. It means meeting CHI's minimum requirements to serve as an Associate Chair (prior AC experience, a track record of CHI reviewing and publications), not actually serving as an AC this year, and not simply being the professor on the paper. The earlier part of the blog only said "one author can take all four"; this constraint surfaces in the FAQ, so check the official qualification policy when you assign slots.

Who is qualified to take a slot?

  • Prior mentoring or training in review writing

  • Prior AC or equivalent reviewing leadership experience
  • 8+ CHI full-paper reviews in the past 8 years
  • 5+ HCI full publications, including 2+ CHI full papers
  • 5+ years of professional HCI experience
Exemptions · Aug 24 post
  • No qualified author on the paper team (declare at submission)
  • Parental leave
  • Medical emergency
  • Busy schedules / ordinary workload do not qualify

Stage 2 · Screening · notifications ~Oct 25

Screening before full review: Desk Reject and Assisted Desk Reject

The official structure is: screening check, then Desk Reject, then the Assisted Desk Reject phase. Desk Reject is for submissions that cannot proceed because they fail basic requirements: incomplete submissions, anonymization violations, undeclared concurrent submissions, wrong format, out of scope, not in English, ACM policy violations. An automated tool surfaces candidate submissions, but ACs, SCs, and Papers Chairs are responsible for the decisions. Desk-rejected papers are not assigned to external reviewers.

ADR happens after those basic checks and is the genuinely new part. Its purpose, in the official wording, is to identify papers that "appear to have a realistic path to acceptance" and should therefore proceed to full peer review. The AC decides whether a paper receives an ADR outcome, and an ADR recommendation receives additional human oversight before authors are notified. Small inconsistency worth knowing: the current process page says an SC and a Paper Chair review and confirm, while the Aug 17 post says SC review and confirm; the slide stays at "human oversight" rather than resolving that for them. Authors whose papers do not proceed receive written feedback from the AC around October 25.

Two things about the name and the tooling. First, "Assisted" does not mean AI-assisted; it is ACM terminology for the AC or SC assisting the Papers Chairs with the desk-reject decision. Second, the red box: remember slide 3, the process is evolving? This is the concrete example. The Aug 17 post described an AI-assisted ADR rubric; on Aug 29 the chairs announced it will not be used in CHI 2027 peer review. ADR decisions are made by humans.

On the numbers: the working target is 50 to 60 percent of submissions proceeding to full external review, and the chairs stress the goal is not to predetermine an acceptance rate or a fixed number of accepted papers; papers are accepted because they meet CHI's standards. The motivation is workload: roughly 20,000 reviews projected, versus 24,099 reviews at CHI 2026.

Gate 1Desk Reject (DR)

  • For submissions that cannot proceed to review because they fail basic requirements
  • Examples: incomplete submission, anonymization violations, undeclared concurrent submissions, incorrect submission category / format, clearly unfinished papers, or ACM authorship-policy violations
  • An automated screening tool surfaces candidate submissions for human inspection
  • ACs, SCs, and Papers Chairs are responsible for desk-reject decisions
  • Desk-rejected submissions are not assigned to external reviewers

Gate 2 · NewAssisted Desk Reject (ADR)

  • Happens after the basic desk-reject checks
  • Purpose: identify papers that “appear to have a realistic path to acceptance” and should proceed to full peer review
  • The AC is responsible for deciding whether a paper receives an ADR outcome
  • An ADR recommendation receives additional human oversight before authors are notified
  • Authors whose papers do not proceed receive written feedback from the AC around Oct 25
Aug 29 update

The AI-assisted ADR rubric will not be used by ACs in CHI 2027 peer review; it is being tested only.

Working target: ~50–60% proceed to full external review after DR and ADR; not a predetermined acceptance rate or quota. ~20,000 reviews projected, compared with 24,099 at CHI 2026.

Sources: Papers Review Process page; process post (Aug 17); Aug 29 update
Stage 2 · Screening

Automated & AI-assisted tools in CHI 2027

Important distinction: automation, AI, and LLMs are not the same thing.

One thing to make explicit on this page: automated does not mean AI, and AI does not mean LLM. The completeness checker is rule-based. The matching system uses keyword-based matching. The desk-reject support combines deterministic and model-based checks. The explicitly AI-assisted ADR rubric is the one that will not be used for CHI 2027 decisions.

Three tools actually run in 2027. The completeness check is rule-based and deterministic: it checks review-responsibility slots, ORCID and DBLP identifiers, and descriptors; the chairs state explicitly that no LLM is involved.

Matching identifies potentially suitable ACs and reviewers; reviewer suggestions are advisory and the AC chooses the reviewer team. Desk-reject support surfaces candidate submissions for human inspection; in the official wording, "a flag is not a decision": the AC examines the paper and an SC confirms before any desk reject is issued.

Tool 4 is this page's nuance: it is not "gone", it is "no, testing only". The AI-assisted ADR rubric report is not used by ACs in CHI 2027 peer review, but it is still being tested.

And close with the official core statement, verbatim: "No AI system decides whether a CHI 2027 paper is accepted or rejected." Humans retain responsibility and authority for consequential decisions.

ToolUsed in CHI 2027?What it does / does not do
1 · Submission completeness checkYesChecks review-responsibility slots, ORCID/DBLP identifiers, and descriptors; rule-based, no LLM
2 · Paper–AC/reviewer matchingYesKeyword/IDF-based matching; identifies suitable ACs/reviewers, and the AC chooses reviewers
3 · Desk-reject supportYesMix of deterministic and model-based checks; only flags candidates for human inspection
4 · AI-assisted ADR rubric reportNo — testing onlyAI-assisted rubric; not used by ACs in CHI 2027 peer review

More importantly: no AI system decides whether a CHI 2027 paper is accepted or rejected. Humans retain responsibility and authority for consequential decisions.

Source: “AI-assisted tools in the CHI 2027 papers review process” (Aug 29)
Stage 3 · Peer review

How does reviewer matching work?

First, what changed structurally. Authors no longer pick a topical subcommittee at submission; that fixed container is gone, though Subcommunity Chairs still provide oversight across groups of ACs. And AC bidding is replaced by automated keyword-based matching: bidding across 7,000 papers is unworkable, and the chairs name it as a collusion-ring risk.

Authors describe the expertise needed to review the paper on four facets: domain, method or approach, the users and communities involved, and the contribution type. The message to take home: choose descriptors based on what expertise is needed to review the paper, not simply what the paper is about. The old keyword system had broken down; "Qualitative Methods" alone was ticked by almost a quarter of submissions.

The flow on the right: descriptors plus reviewer and AC expertise profiles feed automated matching. Per the May 28 post, descriptors are one signal among several; matching also weighs the paper text, conflicts, workload, and reviewer qualifications, under human oversight. The paper is matched to an AC, the system suggests three candidate reviewers, and then come the two human control points. One: the AC has final authority over reviewer selection; the suggestions are not locked in, the AC can replace them or find different reviewers. Two: the reviewer verifies expertise fit; the official review-process page says that if your expertise rating on a submission would be 1, No Knowledge, you should decline.

On declines: a replacement paper is usually offered, and completing it fulfills the slot. If no suitable replacement is found, per the Aug 17 FAQ the decline does not affect the submission's status. Repeated or unjustified declines, though, fall under the Review Responsibility Policy; the official wording is actually stronger, they can lead to the reviewer's own submission being desk-rejected.

What changed
  • No author-selected topical subcommittee
  • No AC bidding; replaced by keyword-based matching
  • SCs still provide oversight across groups of ACs

Authors describe the expertise needed

Paper descriptors · 4 facets
  • Domain
  • Method / approach
  • Users, participants, communities
  • Primary contribution

Choose descriptors based on the expertise needed to review the paper, not every topic the paper mentions.

Stage 3 · Peer review

Paper descriptors: what authors provide

This is the actual PCS form. The framing sentence at the top is the key: imagine the keyword list is preceded by "a reviewer judging my work should have expertise related to". You are tagging the expertise needed to assess your contribution, not describing your submission.

The counts are fixed: two to six Domain keywords, one or two Method/Approach, zero to two Users (only if a specific population is the focus), and exactly one Primary Contribution. The tags are matched against reviewers' self-rated expertise, and there is a keyword finder tool for browsing the full list.

“A reviewer judging my work should have expertise related to…”

  • Tag the expertise needed to assess your contribution, not what the submission is about
  • Domain: 2–6
  • Method / Approach: 1–2
  • Users: 0–2, only if a specific population is the focus
  • Primary Contribution: exactly 1
  • Matched against reviewers' self-rated expertise; the keyword finder tool helps browse the list

Screenshot: PCS submission form (keywords step)

Sources: PCS submission system; reviewer-matching post (May 28)
Stage 3 · Peer review

Expertise descriptors: what reviewers provide

The reviewer side of the same vocabulary. You rate your expertise per area on a four-level scale, and every rating draws on a shared budget of 65 points: Expert costs 5, Competent 2, Limited 1, None is the free default.

Two things to stress. A tag states both your knowledge and how much you are willing to commit to reviewing in that area. And because Expert costs disproportionately more, reserve it for areas of real expertise you genuinely want to review; you do not need to spend the whole budget.

Expert means published in the area within the last five years; Competent means you can give reviewer input on at least some topics; Limited means some advice but not on specifics; None means not enough experience to comfortably advise.

A shared budget of 65 points: Expert 5 · Competent 2 · Limited 1 · None 0

  • Expert (5): published in this area within the last 5 years
  • Competent (2): can give reviewer input on some topics in the area
  • Limited (1): some advice, but not on specifics
  • None (0, default)
  • A tag states knowledge and willingness to review there; reserve Expert for areas you genuinely want to review
  • How the expertise areas were developed: chi.acm.org/review-descriptors

Stage 3 · Peer review

Full peer review: 3 external reviews + 1 AC meta-review

A new AC model

For papers that make it into full review: three substantive external reviews plus one AC meta-review. Careful with the framing: this is not four equivalent reviews or four votes. The AC is the review manager and synthesizer, and the meta-review is formed on top of the external reviews and the discussion.

One AC manages each paper, about fifteen papers per AC, replacing the previous 1AC/2AC model. The AC selects the external reviewers, reads the paper and the reviews, leads the reviewer discussion, works through disagreements, and writes the meta-review. SCs, each overseeing roughly ten to fifteen ACs, monitor review quality, consistency, fairness, and process integrity.

And new this year: the Emergency Review Board. Experienced reviewers who can step in during the final two weeks when assigned reviews do not arrive, so one missing review does not sink a paper's timeline.

3+1

3 substantive external reviews + 1 AC meta-review

One AC manages each paper, replacing the previous 1AC / 2AC model

Who does what

  • One AC per paper (~15 papers each): selects external reviewers, reads the paper and reviews, leads reviewer discussion, works through disagreements, and writes the meta-review
  • SCs (each overseeing ~10–15 ACs) monitor review quality, consistency, fairness, and process integrity
  • Emergency Review Board (ERB): experienced reviewers can step in during the final two weeks when assigned reviews do not arrive
Sources: process post (Aug 17) · Papers Review Process page
Stage 3 · Peer review

How should reviewers evaluate a CHI paper?

The primary question on the review form is simple: does the paper make a strong contribution to HCI? Reviewers assess it across five dimensions: originality (new ideas or approaches, a clear contribution to HCI), correctness (clear processes, rigor by the subfield's own definition), novelty (prior work adequately reviewed, sufficiently novel versus the state of the art), importance (why the contribution and benefit matter, and how much), and clarity of exposition.

Reviewers make a recommendation on the review form using five options, worded as: I recommend Accept with Minor Revisions (A); I can go with either Accept with Minor Revisions or Revise and Resubmit (ARR); I recommend Revise and Resubmit (RR); I can go with either Reject or Revise and Resubmit (RRX); I recommend Reject (X). These are reviewer recommendations, not final decision categories.

What makes a good review: it evaluates the work on its own aims, methods, and scholarly tradition, rather than the reviewer's preferred way of doing research. It is specific, actionable, respectful, and well justified, it clearly states the revisions needed, and typically lands around 650 words.

The reassuring takeaway for the room: the reviewing criteria are largely continuous with CHI 2026. The major changes this year are in how reviews are assigned, managed, and used, not in what counts as good work.

Primary question

Does the paper make a strong contribution to HCI?

Assess across five dimensions
  • Originality: What new ideas or approaches are introduced? We want to emphasize that an acceptable paper must make a clear contribution to HCI.
  • Correctness: How clear are the authors’ processes? How rigorous is the research (for the subfield’s definition of rigor)?
  • Novelty: Is prior work adequately reviewed? Is the current work sufficiently novel in comparison to the state-of-the-art?
  • Importance: Why do the contribution and benefit matter, and how much?
  • Clarity of exposition: Is the paper clearly written?
External reviewer recommendations
  • I recommend Accept with Minor Revisions. (A)
  • I can go with either Accept with Minor Revisions or Revise and Resubmit. (ARR)
  • I recommend Revise and Resubmit. (RR)
  • I can go with either Reject or Revise and Resubmit. (RRX)
  • I recommend Reject. (X)
A good review · Guide to Reviewing Papers

Specific, actionable, respectful, and well justified; typically around 650 words.

The reviewing criteria are largely continuous with CHI 2026; the major changes are in how reviews are assigned, managed, and used.

Source: CHI 2027 Papers Review Process page
Stage 4 · First decisions · reviews released Nov 5

How does the Round 1 decision work?

Once the reviews arrive, the AC leads the reviewer discussion, works through disagreements, and writes the meta-review. That produces one of three first-round paths.

If someone asks how the PC meeting works: there is no single fixed format this year. Each SC decides how their subcommunity deliberates; some may hold a synchronous meeting, others run entirely asynchronously on PCS, others somewhere in between, and the chairs explicitly give SCs autonomy over size, time zone, synchronicity, and tools. PC meetings happen at the end of October, and the AC's meta-review, informed by both the external reviews and the discussion, forms the basis for the first-round outcome.

Minor revisions: all three reviews at ARR or better, a clear path to acceptance, and the revision is checked by the AC only, no re-review. Major revisions: majority-positive reviews but substantial changes; the revision goes back to the reviewers, and rejection is still possible. Reject: below the revise-and-resubmit threshold, but authors still receive all reviews plus the meta-review.

Both revision paths get exactly four weeks, and the second round can only end in accept or reject; there is no second round of major revisions.

Reviews arrive→ AC-led reviewer discussion→ AC meta-review→ First-round outcome

Deliberation format varies by SC: a synchronous PC meeting, fully asynchronous on PCS, or in between (end of October).

Outcome 1Minor revisions

  • All three reviews at ARR or better: clear path to acceptance
  • Revision checked by the AC only, no re-review

Outcome 2Major revisions

  • Majority-positive reviews, but substantial changes needed
  • Revision goes back to the reviewers; rejection still possible

Outcome 3Reject

  • Below the revise-and-resubmit threshold
  • Authors still receive all reviews + the AC meta-review

Both revision paths get 4 weeks. The second round ends in exactly Accept or Reject; there is no second round of major revisions.

Sources: process post (Aug 17) · Papers Review Process page
Stage 5 · Revision & final decisions · Dec 3 / Dec 17

Revise, resubmit, and the final decision

Mechanics of the revision: highlight your changes in the document, write a response letter, and note the author list is frozen at submission; you cannot add or remove anyone.

If reviewer instructions are unclear, you can message the AC anonymously through the submission system; genuinely useful, people rarely know it exists.

Minor track: the AC verifies the bounded changes. Major track: the original reviewers reassess (new reviewers may be added but get the full history) and the AC writes the final summary. December 17 you get accept or reject with the complete review record. There is no third round.

After minor revisionsAC checks your revision

  • The AC verifies the specific, bounded changes
  • No new external reviews

After major revisionsReviewers re-review

  • The original reviewers assess the revision (new ones may be added with full context)
  • The AC writes the final summary
  • Revisions need highlighted changes and a response letter; the author list is frozen
  • Authors can communicate anonymously with the AC through the submission system
Accept or Reject Final decisions with the complete review record on Dec 17, 2026. No third round.
Sources: process post (Aug 17) · Papers Review Process page
Recap

What actually changed, side by side

Pulling it all together, side by side. [Walk the table row by row.]

Two rows deserve care. The review composition: 2026 had a 1AC/2AC pair plus two external reviewers, with the 2AC writing a substantive full review; 2027 replaces that with one AC plus a third external reviewer, and the AC writes the meta-review. And the screening row: ADR is not new in 2027; CHI 2026 already used it on a limited scale, around 7 percent of submissions. What changes is the scale of staged screening, from about 86 percent reaching full review to a working target of 50 to 60 percent.

The through-line: every one of these changes is about scaling human attention. Fewer papers in full review, one accountable AC, matching instead of subcommittee selection and bidding, and authors formally sharing the reviewing load.

Whether that trade-off is the right one is exactly what I'd like to discuss in a minute; hold that thought.

Until CHI 2026CHI 2027
1AC + 2AC + 2 external reviewers1 AC + 3 external reviewers, with SC oversight
Authors select topical subcommittees; ACs bidNo author-selected topical subcommittee; descriptor-based matching
~86% sent to full review; ADR used on a limited scaleWorking target ~50–60% proceed to full review after DR + ADR
Keywords primarily describe the paper4-facet descriptors describe the expertise needed to review it
No review requirement tied to submission4 review-responsibility slots per submission
Replacement reviews handled ad hoc by ACs/SCsEmergency Review Board for late review gaps
Sources: Aug 17 · May 28 · Aug 24 posts
Beyond papers · Posters

Poster submissions

One more track worth knowing about, because the review-responsibility model extends there too. Posters are due January 21, 2027, notification February 18; up to four pages excluding references, anonymous, single-column ACM template.

The headline: poster authors must also designate four review-responsibility slots, filled by authors of the submission, for the Posters track. Declared reviewers update their PCS profiles and participate in bidding; assignments are automatic. If any assigned review is not completed by the deadline, the poster is desk-rejected with no feedback. The chairs explicitly encourage distributing the reviewing fairly and not overburdening early-career researchers.

Selection is an ACM Reviewed process with light feedback. The criteria look familiar (originality, importance, novelty, correctness, clarity) plus two poster-specific ones: discussibility, and the visual poster presentation. And completeness of the work is explicitly not a direct criterion; the track is meant to encourage nascent research.

Key facts · Posters page
  • Submission deadline: Jan 21, 2027 (AoE) · notification Feb 18, 2027
  • Up to 4 pages (excluding references), anonymous, single-column ACM template
  • ACM Reviewed process with light feedback
  • Familiar criteria plus Discussibility and Visual Poster Presentation
  • Completeness is not a direct criterion: the track encourages nascent research

Review responsibility applies here too

  • Poster authors must designate four review-responsibility slots for the Posters track, filled by authors of the submission
  • Declared reviewers update their PCS profiles and participate in bidding; review assignments are made automatically
  • Failure to complete an assigned review by the deadline → desk rejection of the poster, no feedback
  • Distribute the reviewing ethically and fairly; avoid overburdening early-career researchers
Source: CHI 2027 Posters page · Review Responsibility
